# Lab 11: Server Resources and Scaling {.unnumbered} :::: {.callout-warning collapse='false' appearance='default' icon='false'} ## [Caution]{style='font-weight: bold; font-size: 1.25em;'} ::: {style='font-size: 1.00em; color: var(--callout-body-color, #282b2d);'} This section is being revised. Thank you for your patience. ::: :::: How big does a server need to be? Three resources decide: CPU, RAM, and storage, plus a GPU for some modeling work. The examples come from the `t3.micro` we've been running since [Lab 7](lab07.qmd); scaling it up when it runs short is covered in [Instance Size](instance-size.qmd). ## How computers work (for data science) Each comprehension question below asks which part of a computer we'd upgrade to fix a problem. To answer them, it helps to know what each part does. The chapter explains the parts from a system administrator's point of view. The sections below add the R and Python side, with links to Wikipedia for more depth. ### The CPU The [central processing unit (CPU)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Central_processing_unit) is the part of the computer that runs your code. Every program, from a Python script to the operating system, is a long list of small instructions. The CPU works through that list in a cycle: ```{mermaid} %%| fig-cap: 'The CPU Instruction Cycle' %%| fig-width: 7.0 %%| fig-align: 'center' %%{init: {'theme': 'base', 'themeVariables': {'fontFamily': 'monospace', 'fontSize':'13px', 'lineColor':'#999999', 'transitionColor':'#999999'}}}%% stateDiagram-v2 Fetch: Fetch the next instruction from RAM Execute: Execute the instruction Store: Store the result [*] --> Fetch Fetch --> Execute Execute --> Store Store --> Fetch ``` Each trip around this cycle takes a tiny fraction of a second. The number of cycles per second is the clock speed, measured in gigahertz (GHz). A 3 GHz CPU runs about three billion cycles each second. A higher clock speed means each step of your code finishes sooner. R and Python add a layer between our code and the CPU. Both are interpreted languages, so each line we write turns into many CPU instructions while it runs. Vectorized functions skip most of that work by handing the whole job to compiled C code. The two versions below give the same answer. On my laptop, with a vector of 10 million numbers, the vectorized one runs about 90 times faster in both R and Python: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code code-fold="false"} x <- runif(1e7) # loop: the interpreter handles every element total <- 0 for (i in seq_along(x)) total <- total + x[i] # vectorized: one call to compiled code total <- sum(x) ``` ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.python .cell-code code-fold="false"} import numpy as np x = np.random.rand(10_000_000) # loop: the interpreter handles every element total = 0.0 for value in x: total += value # vectorized: one call to compiled code total = x.sum() ``` ::: Before paying for a faster CPU, it's worth looking for loops like these. Rewriting a loop takes a few minutes; a bigger instance costs money every hour it runs. ### Cores A core is a complete processing unit inside the CPU. A CPU with more than one core is a [multi-core processor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Multi-core_processor). Each core runs its own list of instructions, so a four core CPU can work on four tasks at once. Extra cores only help when the work splits into independent pieces: ```{mermaid} %%| fig-cap: 'Splitting a Job Across Cores' %%| fig-width: 7.0 %%| fig-align: 'center' %%{init: {'theme': 'base', 'themeVariables': {'fontFamily': 'monospace', 'fontSize':'13px'}}}%% flowchart TD Job(["One job"]) Split{"Can the job split into
independent pieces?"} subgraph Many["Four cores"] C1("Core 1") C2("Core 2") C3("Core 3") C4("Core 4") end One("One core does all the work
while the others sit idle") Join(["Combine the results"]) Job --> Split Split -->|"Yes"| C1 & C2 & C3 & C4 C1 & C2 & C3 & C4 --> Join Split -->|"No"| One ``` Most R and Python code runs on a single core unless we tell it otherwise (with packages like [`{future}` in R](https://future.futureverse.org/) or [`multiprocessing` in Python](https://docs.python.org/3/library/multiprocessing.html)). **If each step depends on the result of the step before it, the extra cores have nothing to do. This is why faster cores often help more than more cores.** We can check how many cores R and Python can see: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code code-fold="false"} parallel::detectCores() ``` ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.python .cell-code code-fold="false"} import os os.cpu_count() ``` ::: Both return 2 on the `t3.micro`, but that count is threads, not cores. AWS sells virtual CPUs (vCPUs), and each vCPU is one hardware thread. The `t3.micro` has one physical core running two threads, so it shows up as 2 vCPUs. Some modeling packages use every core without being asked. In R, [`{ranger}`](https://imbs-hl.github.io/ranger/) grows random forest trees on all available cores by default. In Python, [`scikit-learn`](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/index.html) models with an `n_jobs` argument use every core when we set `n_jobs=-1`. Parallel work has a RAM cost, too. Each worker process usually gets its own copy of the data, so four workers can need close to four times the memory of one. ### RAM [Random access memory (RAM)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Random-access_memory) holds the data and code the CPU is using right now. RAM is like the top of a desk: everything on it is within arm's reach, but the space is limited. RAM is fast because the CPU can read any location in it directly. It's also temporary, so everything in RAM disappears when the computer turns off. ```{mermaid} %%| fig-cap: 'Loading Data into RAM' %%| fig-width: 7.0 %%| fig-align: 'center' %%{init: {'theme': 'base', 'themeVariables': {'fontFamily': 'monospace', 'fontSize':'13px'}}}%% flowchart TD Load(["Load a dataset"]) Fit{"Does it fit
in RAM?"} Work("The analysis runs") Crash(["The session crashes"]) Load --> Fit Fit -->|"Yes"| Work Fit -->|"No"| Crash ``` When we load a dataset in R or Python, the whole thing is copied into RAM. If it doesn't fit, the session doesn't just slow down; it crashes. RAM is usually the first resource a data science workload runs out of. The `t3.micro` we've been using has only 1 GB. A dataset can take up much more room in RAM than it does on disk. Text columns are the usual cause, along with the temporary copies R and Python make while transforming data. We can measure how much memory an object is using with [`lobstr::obj_size()`](https://lobstr.r-lib.org/reference/obj_size.html) or [`df.memory_usage()`](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/reference/api/pandas.DataFrame.memory_usage.html): ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code code-fold="false"} lobstr::obj_size(penguins) ``` ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.python .cell-code code-fold="false"} df.memory_usage(deep=True).sum() # bytes ``` ::: Comparing these numbers to the file size on disk shows how close a dataset is to the limit. The rule of thumb in the first comprehension question leaves room for this gap. ### Storage [Storage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Computer_data_storage) (a hard drive or solid state drive) keeps files for the long term. If RAM is the desk, storage is the filing cabinet across the room. It holds far more, and it keeps everything when the power is off. The trade off is speed: reading from even a fast solid state drive takes about a thousand times longer than reading from RAM. ```{mermaid} %%| fig-cap: 'Speed and Size Trade Off' %%| fig-width: 7.0 %%| fig-align: 'center' %%{init: {'theme': 'base', 'themeVariables': {'fontFamily': 'monospace', 'fontSize':'13px'}}}%% flowchart TD subgraph Proc["Runs the code"] Cpu("CPU") end subgraph Mem["Fast, small, temporary"] Ram[("RAM")] end subgraph Disk["Slower, large, permanent"] Store[("Storage")] end Proc <--> Mem <--> Disk ``` Because storage is slower, the computer copies data into RAM before the CPU works on it. On an EC2 instance, storage is an [Elastic Block Store (EBS)](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/ebs/latest/userguide/what-is-ebs.html) volume attached to the server. We can make the volume bigger without changing the instance type. Data science projects fill storage faster than we might expect. Package libraries, virtual environments, saved models, and data files all live there. A single deep learning package like [PyTorch](https://pytorch.org/) can take up several gigabytes on its own. We can see how much room the `renv` and `uv` package caches are using with `du`: ::: {.cell} ```{.bash .cell-code code-fold="false"} du -sh ~/.cache/R ~/.cache/uv ``` ::: File format matters, too. A [Parquet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apache_Parquet) file is usually much smaller than the same data saved as a CSV. [R (`{arrow}`)](https://arrow.apache.org/docs/r/) and [Python (`pyarrow`)](https://arrow.apache.org/docs/python/) also read it faster, because the data is compressed and stored by column. ### GPUs A [graphics processing unit (GPU)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Graphics_processing_unit) is a processor built from thousands of small, simple cores. GPUs were designed to draw graphics, which means running the same calculation on millions of pixels at once. Training a deep learning model involves the same kind of math (large matrix multiplications). A GPU's thousands of cores can finish that work in hours instead of days. ```{mermaid} %%| fig-cap: 'CPU and GPU Cores' %%| fig-width: 7.0 %%| fig-align: 'center' %%{init: {'theme': 'base', 'themeVariables': {'fontFamily': 'monospace', 'fontSize':'13px'}}}%% flowchart TD subgraph Cpu["CPU: a few strong cores"] direction LR c1("core") ~~~ c2("core") ~~~ c3("core") ~~~ c4("core") end subgraph Gpu["GPU: many small cores"] direction LR g0("core") ~~~ g1("core") ~~~ g2("core") ~~~ g3("core") ~~~ g4("core") ~~~ g5("core") g6("core") ~~~ g7("core") ~~~ g8("core") ~~~ g9("core") ~~~ g10("core") ~~~ g11("core") g12("core") ~~~ g13("core") ~~~ g14("core") ~~~ g15("core") ~~~ g16("core") ~~~ g17("core") end Cpu ~~~ Gpu classDef big font-size:18px classDef small font-size:12px class c1,c2,c3,c4 big class g0,g1,g2,g3,g4,g5,g6,g7,g8,g9,g10,g11,g12,g13,g14,g15,g16,g17 small ``` GPUs come with three catches: 1. They're expensive. 2. Our code has to be written (or configured) to use one. 3. Code that runs one step at a time gets nothing from a GPU. Most of the data science toolkit never touches a GPU. [`{dplyr}`](https://dplyr.tidyverse.org/), [`{pandas}`](https://pandas.pydata.org/), and most of [`{tidymodels}`](https://www.tidymodels.org/) and [`scikit-learn`](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/) run on the CPU. GPUs matter for deep learning frameworks like [PyTorch](https://pytorch.org/) and [TensorFlow](https://www.tensorflow.org/) (and their R interfaces, [`{torch}`](https://torch.mlverse.org/) and [`{keras3}`](https://keras3.posit.co/)), and for a few model libraries like [XGBoost](https://xgboost.readthedocs.io/). In each case we check that the GPU is visible, then move the work onto it: ::: {.cell} ```{.python .cell-code code-fold="false"} import torch torch.cuda.is_available() #<1> device = "cuda" if torch.cuda.is_available() else "cpu" model = model.to(device) #<2> ``` ::: 1. `True` if `PyTorch` can see a GPU 2. Move the model's weights onto the GPU ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code code-fold="false"} library(torch) cuda_is_available() #<1> ``` ::: 1. `TRUE` if `torch` can see a GPU A GPU also has its [own memory (VRAM)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Video_random-access_memory), separate from the server's RAM. The model and each batch of data have to fit in VRAM, which brings back the same "does it fit?" question from the RAM section. ### How the parts work together The diagram below follows data through a typical analysis: ```{mermaid} %%| fig-cap: 'How the Parts Work Together' %%| fig-width: 7.0 %%| fig-align: 'center' %%{init: {'theme': 'base', 'themeVariables': {'fontFamily': 'monospace', 'fontSize':'13px'}}}%% sequenceDiagram participant S as Storage participant R as RAM participant C as CPU or GPU S->>R: Loads the data R->>C: Reads the data C->>C: Runs the computation C->>R: Writes the results R->>S: Saves the results ``` Data starts in storage, gets copied into RAM, and is processed by the CPU (or GPU). The results go back into RAM, and we save them to storage when we want to keep them. Each comprehension question below describes a bottleneck at one of these steps. In a typical R or Python script, each step maps to a familiar function call: | Step | R | Python | |---|---|---| | Storage to RAM | `readr::read_csv()` | `pd.read_csv()` | | CPU work | `dplyr::mutate()`, `lm()` | `df.assign()`, `model.fit()` | | RAM to storage | `arrow::write_parquet()`, `saveRDS()` | `df.to_parquet()`, `joblib.dump()` | ## Comprehension questions > "*Think about the scenarios below. Which part of your computer would you want to upgrade to solve the problem?*" > > "1. *You try to load a `.csv` file into `{pandas}` in Python. It churns for a while and then crashes.*" RAM. `{pandas}` loads the whole file into memory, and transformations make temporary copies on top of that. When the data doesn't fit, the session crashes instead of slowing down. **The chapter's rule of thumb is to have at least three times as much RAM as the largest dataset**: $$\text{Amount of RAM} \ge 3 \times \text{max amount of data}$$ Before buying more, it's worth asking whether the whole file needs to be in memory at once. Reading only some columns, or switching to a database or Parquet file, can load far less. With a 400 MB file as an example, the 3x rule already asks for more memory than a `t3.micro` has: ```{mermaid} %%| fig-cap: 'RAM Needed for a 400 MB CSV (illustrative)' %%| fig-width: 7.0 %%| fig-align: 'center' %%{init: {'theme': 'base', 'themeVariables': {'fontFamily': 'monospace', 'xyChart': {'plotColorPalette': '#2A6F77'}}}}%% xychart-beta title "Loading a 400 MB CSV on a t3.micro" x-axis ["CSV on disk", "RAM needed (3x)", "t3.micro RAM"] y-axis "Gigabytes" 0 --> 1.5 bar [0.4, 1.2, 1.0] ``` > "2. *You go to build a new ML model on your data. You'd like to re-train the model once a day, but training this model takes 26 hours on your laptop.*" A faster CPU (or a GPU). A 26 hour job can't run once a day no matter how much RAM or storage the machine has. If the model is parallel (deep learning or tree based models like XGBoost), a GPU is the upgrade that turns days into hours. The chapter's advice is to try faster CPU cores first. The order to try things in looks like this: ```{mermaid} %%| fig-cap: 'Speeding Up a Training Job' %%| fig-width: 7.0 %%| fig-align: 'center' %%{init: {'theme': 'base', 'themeVariables': {'fontFamily': 'monospace', 'fontSize':'13px'}}}%% flowchart TD Job(["Training takes 26 hours"]) Fast("Faster CPU cores
C family instance") Check{"Fits in a day?"} Par{"Highly parallel model?
deep learning, trees"} GPU("GPU instance
P family, set in the code") Done(["Retrain daily"]) Rethink("Rethink the job
less data, fewer features") Job --> Fast --> Check Check --"yes"--> Done Check --"no"--> Par Par --"yes"--> GPU --> Done Par --"no"--> Rethink style Job fill:#D2562B,stroke:#fff,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff style Fast fill:#2A6F77,stroke:#fff,stroke-width:1px,color:#fff style Check fill:#E8A33D,stroke:#000,stroke-width:1px,color:#000 style Par fill:#E8A33D,stroke:#000,stroke-width:1px,color:#000 style GPU fill:#5B8C5A,stroke:#fff,stroke-width:1px,color:#fff style Rethink fill:#666,stroke:#999,stroke-width:1px,color:#fff style Done fill:#1B2A41,stroke:#fff,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff ``` > "3. *You design a visualization using the `{matplotlib}` package and want to create one version of the visualization for each US state. You could do it in a loop, but it would be faster to parallelize the plot creation. Right now, you're running on a `t2.small` with 1 CPU.*" More CPU cores. Parallelizing means running several plots at the same time, one per core, and a single core can only run one at a time. Fifty plots on one core is still a loop. A GPU doesn't help here because `{matplotlib}` draws on the CPU. Assume each plot takes one minute. With the same total work, four cores finish in about a quarter of the time: ```{mermaid} %%| fig-cap: 'One Core vs. Four Cores (illustrative)' %%| fig-width: 8.0 %%| fig-align: 'center' %%{init: {'theme': 'base', 'themeVariables': {'fontFamily': 'monospace', 'fontSize':'13px', 'taskBkgColor':'#2A6F77', 'taskBorderColor':'#2A6F77', 'taskTextColor':'#ffffff', 'taskTextLightColor':'#ffffff', 'taskTextOutsideColor':'#E8A33D', 'sectionBkgColor':'#E8E8E8', 'altSectionBkgColor':'#F5F5F5', 'gridColor':'#999999'}}}%% gantt title 50 plots, one core vs. four dateFormat HH:mm axisFormat %H:%M section 1 core 1 to 13 :a1, 00:00, 13m 14 to 26 :a2, after a1, 13m 27 to 38 :a3, after a2, 12m 39 to 50 :a4, after a3, 12m section 4 cores 1 to 13 :b1, 00:00, 13m 14 to 26 :b2, 00:00, 13m 27 to 38 :b3, 00:00, 12m 39 to 50 :b4, 00:00, 12m ``` > "*Draw a mind map of the following: CPU, RAM, Storage, Operations Per Second, Parallel Operations, GPU, Machine Learning.*" The chapter's analogy is a factory that does addition problems. The CPU is the assembly line, RAM is the space next to the line where work waits, and storage is the warehouse next door. The mind map groups the other terms under the resource they describe: ```{mermaid} %%| fig-cap: 'Server Resources Mind Map' %%| fig-width: 8.0 %%| fig-align: 'center' %%{init: {'theme': 'base', 'themeVariables': {'fontFamily': 'monospace', 'fontSize':'13px'}}}%% mindmap root((Server resources)) CPU Few fast cores Operations Per Second GPU Many slow cores Parallel Operations Machine Learning RAM Data being worked on Wiped on restart Storage Saved files and packages Slow but permanent ``` > "*What are the architectural differences between a CPU and a GPU? Why does this make a GPU particularly good for Machine Learning?*" A CPU has a handful of fast cores, usually 4 to 16 on a laptop. A GPU has hundreds or thousands of slow ones: 700 to 4,000 on a mid range card, each running at 1 to 10 percent of a CPU core's speed. The CPU is built to finish one problem quickly. The GPU is built to work on thousands of small problems at once. Training most machine learning models is that kind of work. The same arithmetic repeats over many rows, weights, or trees, and each piece is independent of the others. When work splits that way, the number of cores matters more than the speed of any one core. A GPU can then train in hours what a CPU trains in days. Step by step R and Python code is the opposite case, so it runs better on fewer, faster CPU cores. Placing each chip by core count and core speed shows why they suit different work: ```{mermaid} %%| fig-cap: 'CPU vs. GPU Cores' %%| fig-width: 7.0 %%| fig-align: 'center' %%{init: {'theme': 'base', 'themeVariables': {'fontFamily': 'monospace', 'fontSize':'13px', 'quadrant1Fill':'#1B2A41', 'quadrant2Fill':'#2A6F77', 'quadrant3Fill':'#1B2A41', 'quadrant4Fill':'#5B8C5A', 'quadrant1TextFill':'#ffffff', 'quadrant2TextFill':'#ffffff', 'quadrant3TextFill':'#ffffff', 'quadrant4TextFill':'#ffffff', 'quadrantPointFill':'#E8A33D', 'quadrantPointTextFill':'#ffffff', 'quadrantInternalBorderStrokeFill':'#ffffff', 'quadrantExternalBorderStrokeFill':'#999999'}}}%% quadrantChart title Core count vs. core speed x-axis Few cores --> Many cores y-axis Slow cores --> Fast cores quadrant-1 Many and fast quadrant-2 CPU territory quadrant-3 Few and slow quadrant-4 GPU territory t3.micro CPU: [0.12, 0.62] Laptop CPU: [0.15, 0.82] Mid range GPU: [0.85, 0.18] ``` > "*How would you do the following?*" > > "1. *Find all running JupyterHub processes that belong to the user `alexkgold`.*" `ps aux` lists every process with its owner, and `grep` narrows it down: ::: {.cell} ```{.bash .cell-code code-fold="false"} ps aux | grep jupyterhub | grep alexkgold ``` ::: Each `|` passes one command's output to the next, and each `grep` keeps fewer lines: ```{mermaid} %%| fig-cap: 'Filtering ps aux with grep' %%| fig-width: 7.0 %%| fig-align: 'center' %%{init: {'theme': 'base', 'themeVariables': {'fontFamily': 'monospace', 'fontSize':'13px'}}}%% flowchart TD Ps("ps aux
every process, one per line") G1("grep jupyterhub
only lines mentioning jupyterhub") G2("grep alexkgold
only lines owned by alexkgold") Out[/"JupyterHub processes owned by alexkgold"/] Ps -->|"pipe"| G1 -->|"pipe"| G2 --> Out style Ps fill:#2A6F77,stroke:#fff,stroke-width:1px,color:#fff style G1 fill:#2A6F77,stroke:#fff,stroke-width:1px,color:#fff style G2 fill:#2A6F77,stroke:#fff,stroke-width:1px,color:#fff style Out fill:#E8A33D,stroke:#000,stroke-width:1px,color:#000 ``` `ps -u alexkgold` lists only that user's processes, so `ps -u alexkgold | grep jupyterhub` gets to the same place. Our instance doesn't run JupyterHub, but the same pattern finds the app from [Installing a Real Application](install-real-app.qmd), which runs as its service account: ::: {.cell} ```{.bash .cell-code code-fold="false"} ps -u baseball-trajectory -o pid,%cpu,%mem,cmd ``` ::: If one of these processes is running away with the CPU, its PID goes to `kill`. For a `systemd` service, `sudo systemctl restart` is the better tool. > "2. *Find the different disks attached to your server and see how full each one is.*" `lsblk` lists the disks and partitions, and `df -h` shows how full each mounted filesystem is: ::: {.cell} ```{.bash .cell-code code-fold="false"} lsblk df -h ``` ::: On an EC2 instance the root EBS volume usually shows up as `nvme0n1`, mounted at `/`. `-h` prints sizes in K, M, and G instead of blocks. `lsblk` shows the whole tree, including partitions that aren't mounted; `df -h` reports only the mounted ones. On an AL2023 instance the tree usually looks like this: ```{mermaid} %%| fig-cap: 'What lsblk and df -h Show' %%| fig-width: 7.0 %%| fig-align: 'center' %%{init: {'theme': 'base', 'themeVariables': {'fontFamily': 'monospace', 'fontSize':'13px'}}}%% block-beta columns 3 disk["nvme0n1: EBS root volume"]:3 space:3 p1["partition: nvme0n1p1"] p127["partition: nvme0n1p127"] p128["partition: nvme0n1p128"] m1["mounted at /"] b1["BIOS boot, not mounted"] m128["mounted at /boot/efi"] disk --> p1 disk --> p127 disk --> p128 style disk fill:#1B2A41,stroke:#fff,color:#fff style m1 fill:#2A6F77,stroke:#fff,color:#fff style m128 fill:#2A6F77,stroke:#fff,color:#fff style b1 fill:#666,stroke:#999,color:#fff ``` > "3. *Find the biggest files in each user's home directory.*" `du` measures sizes, `sort -rh` puts the biggest first, and `head` keeps the top of the list. Home directories belong to other users, so this needs `sudo`: ::: {.cell} ```{.bash .cell-code code-fold="false"} sudo du -ah /home | sort -rh | head -n 20 ``` ::: `-a` includes files, not just directories. To get a short list per user instead of one combined list, loop over the home directories: ::: {.cell} ```{.bash .cell-code code-fold="false"} for d in /home/*; do echo "== $d" sudo du -ah "$d" | sort -rh | head -n 5 done ``` ::: Each stage of the pipeline narrows the list: ```{mermaid} %%| fig-cap: 'Finding the Biggest Files' %%| fig-width: 7.0 %%| fig-align: 'center' %%{init: {'theme': 'base', 'themeVariables': {'fontFamily': 'monospace', 'fontSize':'13px'}}}%% flowchart TD Home[("/home")] Du("sudo du -ah
size of every file and folder") Sort("sort -rh
biggest first, reads K, M, G") Head("head -n 20
keep the top 20") Out[/"Top 20 files and folders"/] Home --> Du --> Sort --> Head --> Out style Home fill:#666,stroke:#999,stroke-width:1px,color:#fff style Du fill:#2A6F77,stroke:#fff,stroke-width:1px,color:#fff style Sort fill:#2A6F77,stroke:#fff,stroke-width:1px,color:#fff style Head fill:#2A6F77,stroke:#fff,stroke-width:1px,color:#fff style Out fill:#E8A33D,stroke:#000,stroke-width:1px,color:#000 ``` ## Recap 1. CPU speed, core count, RAM, and storage each limit a different kind of work. A GPU helps only with parallel work that the code is told to send to it. 2. RAM runs out first for most data science work. Data takes more room in memory than on disk, so plan for about three times the largest dataset. 3. Extra cores help only when a job splits into independent pieces, and most R and Python code has to be told to use them. 4. `ps`, `lsblk`, `df -h`, and `du` show what a server is running and where its storage went. Resizing the instance is covered in [Instance Size](instance-size.qmd).
